card.keepWhy: An honest question, then a yes.
sources: Luke 1:26-38 (the angel Gabriel sent to Nazareth, a city of Galilee, to a virgin espoused to Joseph; “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee”; she is troubled and wonders what this greeting means; “Fear not, Mary, for thou hast found grace with God”; a son to be named Jesus, Son of the Most High; “How shall this be done, because I know not man?”; “no word shall be impossible with God”; “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word”). Douay-Rheims (Challoner).
Fiat: Latin Vulgate, Luke 1:38 “fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum.” Handmaid: Latin ancilla, Greek doule, a woman servant (Luke 1:38).
Catechism of the Catholic Church 484-511 (the Annunciation; Mary’s free consent), 495 (Mother of God), 971 (devotion to Mary differs from the adoration given to God).
The Angelus: traditional Catholic devotion recalling the Annunciation, prayed at morning, noon and evening, often at the ringing of a bell.
The lily: a traditional symbol of Mary in Annunciation paintings.
check: Mary’s age: Luke gives none. The painting prompt says “about sixteen” and the caption says only “a young woman.” Confirm that is acceptable for the art.

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? has life ever asked you for a yes you didn’t feel ready to give?
options: then sit close. this one is about exactly that.
keep this one for the day it comes.

steps.line: In Nazareth, a small town in Galilee, lived a young woman named Mary. She was promised in marriage to a man named Joseph.
One ordinary day, the angel Gabriel came to her and said, “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.”

steps.q: An angel is standing in her house. How does Mary react to his greeting?
o: She’s deeply troubled, and wonders what it means
She kneels and says yes at once
steps.why: Luke says she was troubled. Even Mary is startled. Saints are allowed to be human.

steps.line: She was troubled. Gabriel said, “Do not be afraid, Mary, you have found grace with God. You will have a son, and name him Jesus.”
Mary asked an honest question: “How can this be?” She wasn’t married yet. Gabriel answered, “Nothing is impossible for God.”

steps.q: Earlier in Luke, the priest Zechariah questions Gabriel too, and is struck silent. Mary questions him and isn’t. What’s the difference?
o: Zechariah asked for proof; Mary asked how
Mary was young, so she was let off
A priest should have known better
steps.why: Zechariah asked “How will I know this?”, wanting a sign. Mary trusted, and asked how it would happen. Same angel, very different question.

steps.q: You’re Mary. Engaged, not yet married, and told you’ll have a child. What’s the real risk in saying yes?
o: Being sent away to live at the Temple
None; a baby was always good news
steps.why: Matthew says Joseph planned to quietly end the engagement until a dream changed his mind. Her yes was not a small one.

steps.line: Then Mary said, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord. Be it done to me according to thy word.” And the angel left her.
Today, in many towns, church bells ring at morning, noon and evening. Some Catholics stop and pray the Angelus, remembering this very moment.
steps.label: today

steps.q: When the Angelus bell rings, how does it traditionally ring?
steps.why: Three strokes, three times, with a Hail Mary in each pause, then nine. In Millet’s painting The Angelus, two farmers stop in a field at that sound.

say: here’s what i love. God doesn’t push. the angel asks, mary asks back, and then she chooses.
catholics honor mary above every other saint, as the mother of God. honor, not worship. and the church treasures her yes because it was free: she asked, she listened, she chose.

steps.q: Gabriel calls Mary “full of grace” before she has said yes to anything. What does that tell you about grace?
o: She earned it by being so good
It only arrives once you say yes
It was already there, before her answer
steps.why: The gift came first, then the yes. That’s yesterday’s word, grace, at work in Nazareth.

today.say: at noon today, or whenever you notice the time, stop for one breath. you can watch, learn the words, or join in with mary’s: “be it done to me according to thy word.” or just say: let it be.
options: lovely. that’s one of the oldest noon pauses there is.
that counts. one honest pause is a yes too.
